directions: Plant against a masonry wall, arbor, or sturdy trellis where the self-clinging adhesive tendrils can grip; this compact sport of Boston ivy carries small, deeply three-lobed leaves that give it a finer, denser texture than the species. Water regularly during the first two seasons while the holdfasts establish, then rely on rainfall except in prolonged drought. Prune in late winter to control spread and keep growth off gutters, windows, or wood siding, since the adhesive pads can damage paint and mortar over time. Expect brilliant scarlet-crimson fall color even in shadier exposures, along with small blue-black berries that draw songbirds.

Give this cultivar the same masonry, stone, or large tree trunk that ordinary Boston ivy needs, since its self-clinging holdfasts can eventually cover a full building facade. Foliage emerges burgundy-purple in spring, holds a dusky reddish-green through summer, and intensifies to deep wine-red before dropping in fall, offering more season-long color interest than the plain green species. Site it away from wood trim, shutters, and gutters, and cut back annually in late winter to keep growth away from rooflines. It tolerates deep shade but colors most vividly with at least a few hours of direct or bright dappled sun.

This far-northern relative of the more familiar pipevines is one of the hardiest Aristolochia species, twining a heavy woody stem up a strong arbor, pergola post, or dead tree where its huge, rounded heart-shaped leaves can reach nearly a foot across. Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist soil with morning sun and afternoon shade to mimic its native forest-edge habitat in Manchuria and the Russian Far East. The small yellow-green pipe-shaped flowers hide beneath the foliage in late spring and are easy to overlook, but the dense curtain of oversized leaves makes an excellent quick shade screen. Established plants are drought-tolerant once rooted but perform best with consistent moisture through the growing season, and the coarse foliage also serves as a larval host for pipevine swallowtail butterflies.

Choose this dwarf selection where a full-size climbing hydrangea vine would overwhelm the space, since it clings by aerial rootlets to a shaded stone wall, tree trunk, or wooden fence but stays noticeably more compact and slower to spread than the species. The proportionally small, finely textured leaves and miniature white lacecap flower clusters in early summer suit a woodland garden or shaded courtyard where a refined scale matters. Grow it in cool, consistently moist, humus-rich soil and protect the root zone with mulch, since it resents hot, dry conditions. Be patient during the first few years while it establishes its clinging rootlets before active climbing begins in earnest.
sources: Great Plant Picks (Elisabeth C. Miller Botanical Garden)
